summary: Describes conventions for using the SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 hash algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax, including with the Digital Signature Algorithm and ECDSA. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: CMS is the format used for signed and encrypted email. When a message is signed, the signer first computes a hash of the content, and the signature covers that hash. This RFC says which names to use for the newer hash functions in that format, and which names to use when the hash is combined with a signature algorithm.

subtitle: How the SHA-2 hash functions are named and encoded when they are used inside signed and encrypted email.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax needs a fixed object identifier for every algorithm it can carry, and none had been assigned for the SHA-2 family of hash functions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC names the four digests and the signature algorithms that combine them with DSA, RSA and ECDSA, and gives the exact bytes to use for each SMIMECapabilities entry.
tldr.outcome: It also settles a long-standing encoding ambiguity: implementations must accept a missing parameters field and a NULL one, but must always generate the missing form, with one exception for RSA signature padding.

today: RFC 5754 is a Proposed Standard on the Internet standards track. It updates RFC 3370, and no RFC in the site index obsoletes it. The document defines no new identifiers and no new algorithms; it only says how the SHA-2 digests are to be named and encoded in CMS.

sections.title: What This Document Adds
sections.content:
This document specifies the algorithm identifiers and the parameters for the message digest algorithms SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, for use with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), which is defined in RFC 5652. The message digest algorithms themselves are defined in the Secure Hash Standard, and reference code is provided in RFC 4634.

It also specifies the algorithm identifiers and parameters for using those four digests with DSA, with RSA (RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5) as specified in RFC 3447, and with ECDSA.

The document defines no new identifiers. They are taken from RFC 3874, RFC 4055 and RFC 5758, and the parameters follow the conventions specified there, so there is no ASN.1 module in this document.

Two structures are used throughout. The various algorithm identifiers use the AlgorithmIdentifier syntax, a SEQUENCE of an algorithm OBJECT IDENTIFIER and an optional parameters field. The SMIMECapabilities attribute values use the SMIMECapability syntax, a SEQUENCE of a capabilityID OBJECT IDENTIFIER and an optional parameters field.

The RFC also notes that RFC 4231 specifies the conventions for the message authentication code algorithms, that is HMAC with SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, which are outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS is the format used for signed and encrypted email. When a message is signed, the signer first computes a hash of the content, and the signature covers that hash. This RFC says which names to use for the newer hash functions in that format, and which names to use when the hash is combined with a signature algorithm.

sections.title: Where the Identifiers Live and How to Encode Them
sections.content:
Digest algorithm identifiers are located in the SignedData digestAlgorithms field, the SignerInfo digestAlgorithm field, the DigestedData digestAlgorithm field and the AuthenticatedData digestAlgorithm field. The object identifiers are taken from RFC 4055. Digest values are located in the DigestedData digest field and in the Message Digest authenticated attribute, and digest values are also input to the signature algorithms.

The AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field is OPTIONAL, and the RFC sets three requirements. Implementations MUST accept SHA2 AlgorithmIdentifiers with absent parameters. They MUST accept SHA2 AlgorithmIdentifiers with NULL parameters. And they MUST generate SHA2 AlgorithmIdentifiers with absent parameters.

The RFC explains why the two encodings exist. There are two possible encodings for the parameters field associated with these object identifiers, and the two alternatives arise from the loss of the OPTIONAL associated with the algorithm identifier parameters when the 1988 syntax for AlgorithmIdentifier was translated into the 1997 syntax. The OPTIONAL was later recovered by a defect report, but by then many people thought that algorithm parameters were mandatory, so some implementations encode parameters as a NULL element while others omit them entirely. The correct encoding is to omit the parameters field. However, when some uses of these algorithms were defined, it was done using NULL parameters rather than absent parameters: PKCS#1 requires that the padding used for RSA signatures, EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5, use SHA2 AlgorithmIdentifiers with NULL parameters, and the requirement to generate SHA2 AlgorithmIdentifiers with absent parameters does not apply to that padding.
sections.plainLanguage: An algorithm name in CMS is followed by an optional parameters field. Because of an accident in the history of the format, some software writes a null value there and some leaves it out. The RFC says a program must accept both, but should always write it without.

sections.title: The Four Message Digest Algorithms
sections.content:
Each of the four digest algorithms has its own object identifier, taken from RFC 4055, and its own SMIMECapabilities attribute value.

SHA-224 has the object identifier joint-iso-itu-t(2) country(16) us(840) organization(1) gov(101) csor(3) nistalgorithm(4) hashalgs(2) 4. Its SMIMECapability is a SEQUENCE whose capabilityID field holds that identifier with absent parameters, and the DER encoding of the SMIMECapability is 30 0b 06 09 60 86 48 01 65 03 04 02 04.

SHA-256 has the same prefix with hashalgs(2) 1, and the DER encoding 30 0b 06 09 60 86 48 01 65 03 04 02 01. SHA-384 has hashalgs(2) 2, with DER encoding 30 0b 06 09 60 86 48 01 65 03 04 02 02. SHA-512 has hashalgs(2) 3, with DER encoding 30 0b 06 09 60 86 48 01 65 03 04 02 03. The parameters for all four follow the convention set out at the start of section 2.
sections.plainLanguage: Each hash function has a fixed name, an object identifier built from a common prefix and a number: 4 for SHA-224, 1 for SHA-256, 2 for SHA-384 and 3 for SHA-512. The RFC also lists the exact bytes to send for each, so that software agrees on the encoding.

sections.title: DSA with SHA-2
sections.content:
RFC 3370 specifies the conventions for DSA with SHA-1 public key algorithm identifiers, parameters, public keys and signature values, and DSA with SHA2 algorithms uses the same conventions for these identifiers, parameters, public keys and signature values. DSA MAY be used with SHA-224 and SHA-256, and the object identifiers are taken from RFC 5758.

DSA has not been specified with SHA-384 and SHA-512, and they are not supported, because the maximum bit length of p, specified as L, is 3072 for DSA. For consistent cryptographic strength, SHA-384 would be used with DSA where L is 7680, and SHA-512 would be used with DSA where L is 15360.

The algorithm identifier for DSA with SHA-224 signature values is id-dsa-with-sha224, and for SHA-256 it is id-dsa-with-sha256. When either of these identifiers is used, the AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field MUST be absent. The SMIMECapabilities attribute value is a SEQUENCE with the capabilityID field holding the relevant identifier with absent parameters, and the DER encodings are 30 0b 06 09 60 86 48 01 65 03 04 03 01 for SHA-224 and 30 0b 06 09 60 86 48 01 65 03 04 03 02 for SHA-256.
sections.plainLanguage: DSA signatures can use the two shorter hash functions, SHA-224 and SHA-256. The two longer ones are left out because the DSA key size they would need is larger than DSA allows.

sections.title: RSA with SHA-2
sections.content:
RFC 3370 specifies the conventions for RSA with SHA-1 public key algorithm identifiers, parameters, public keys and signature values, and RSA with SHA2 algorithms uses the same conventions for these identifiers, parameters, public keys and signature values. RSA (RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5) MAY be used with SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512, and the object identifiers are taken from RFC 4055.

Four identifiers are named: sha224WithRSAEncryption, sha256WithRSAEncryption, sha384WithRSAEncryption and sha512WithRSAEncryption. When any of these four object identifiers appears within an AlgorithmIdentifier, the parameters MUST be NULL. Implementations MUST accept the parameters being absent as well as present.

The SMIMECapabilities attribute value for support is a SEQUENCE with the capabilityID field holding the identifier with NULL parameters, and the DER encoding is given for each of the four.
sections.plainLanguage: RSA signatures work with all four hash functions. Here the parameters field must hold a null value, although a program should still accept the field being left out.

sections.title: ECDSA with SHA-2
sections.content:
RFC 5753 specifies the conventions for ECDSA with SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 public key algorithm identifiers, parameters, public keys and signature values, and the object identifiers are taken from RFC 5758. The four identifiers for the SHA-2 digests are ecdsa-with-SHA224, ecdsa-with-SHA256, ecdsa-with-SHA384 and ecdsa-with-SHA512.

When any of these four object identifiers appears within an AlgorithmIdentifier, the parameters field MUST be absent. That is, the AlgorithmIdentifier SHALL be a SEQUENCE of one component: the OID ecdsa-with-SHA224, ecdsa-with-SHA256, ecdsa-with-SHA384 or ecdsa-with-SHA512.

The SMIMECapabilities attribute value for support is a SEQUENCE with the capabilityID field holding the identifier with absent parameters, and the DER encoding is given for each of the four.
sections.plainLanguage: ECDSA signatures also work with all four hash functions. Here the parameters field is left out entirely, so the algorithm name stands alone in the message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations in RFC 3370, RFC 3874, RFC 4055, RFC 5753 and RFC 5758 apply. The RFC says no new security considerations are introduced as a result of this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: This document only names existing algorithms and says how to encode them, so it adds no new security questions of its own. The rules come from the documents it refers to.

viz.caption: THE THREE RULES FOR THE PARAMETERS FIELD

items.title: Accept absent parameters
items.text: A program must accept an algorithm identifier with no parameters field.

items.title: Accept NULL parameters
items.text: A program must accept an algorithm identifier whose parameters field is NULL.

items.title: Generate absent parameters
items.text: A program must write the algorithm identifier without a parameters field.
